Flexible Zr‑doped hafnium oxide ferroelectric memcapacitive synaptic 
devices for neuromorphic computing

Abstract
Conventional von Neumann architecture-based computing hardware faces high power consumption challenges and the mis-
match between memory and computation performance when handling increasingly large and complex datasets. The rise of 
artificial neural networks (ANN) has driven the development of bio-inspired memory devices, such as artificial synapses, 
offering new opportunities to overcome the limitations of the post-Moore era. Ferroelectric memcapacitors, which store data 
based on capacitive principles, provide advantages such as resistance to read disturbance and low static power consumption 
compared to memristors, making them highly attractive for ANN applications. In this work, we fabricated Zr-doped ­HfO2 
(HZO) ferroelectric memcapacitive synaptic devices on mica substrate featuring a simple metal-ferroelectric-metal struc-
ture. We investigated the impact of bending on the ferroelectric performance and, through finite element analysis, found that 
stress concentration might lead to an increase in grain boundary defects, resulting in excess oxygen vacancies and a slight 
decrease in ferroelectric polarization. Additionally, we studied the memcapacitive characteristics of the HZO ferroelectric 
synaptic devices and successfully obtained the potentiation and depression characteristics. The synaptic plasticity curves 
were also fitted by least squares to obtain asymmetries of 0.030 and 0.068 for the flat and tensile states, respectively. The 
devices demonstrated remarkable neuromorphic computing capabilities, reaching a digital recognition accuracy as high as 
97.63%. Notably, the maximum energy consumption per device was approximately 1.96 nJ in the training process and 4.03 
pJ in the inference process. This study provides new directions for further developing flexible hafnium-based ferroelectric 
materials and devices.
Keywords  Flexible ferroelectric material · Zr-doped hafnium oxide · Memcapacitor · Synaptic characteristics · 
Neuromorphic computing
1  Introduction
In recent years, rapid advancements in technologies such 
as artificial intelligence (AI), cloud computing, and 5G/6G 
communications indicate that humanity is on the brink of 
entering the era of ubiquitous connectivity. Since the post-
Moore era, AI centered on deep learning has exponentially 
increased demands for hardware computational power. As 
data becomes more diverse and complex, the need for effi-
cient data processing continues to grow [1, 2]. Separation of 
processing and storage units is the main feature of traditional 
computing hardware based on the von Neumann architec-
ture. Consequently, processing frequent and large-scale data 
computation leads to a dramatic increase in power consump-
tion. Humans, as the pinnacle of intelligent life on earth, 
possess the ability to adapt and continuously learn, likely 
due to the complexity of the brain. The human brain contains 
billions of neurons interconnected through trillions of syn-
apses, enabling rapid information transmission and real-time 
processing [3]. Additionally, the human brain operates as a 
highly optimized system with ultra-low-power consumption,

even under high parallel workloads. Emulating the brain’s 
information processing methods to develop new neuromor-
phic computing systems is crucial for breakthroughs in the 
post-Moore era, with simulating the function of biological 
synapses being essential.
Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are computational 
models that mimic the structure and function of biological 
neural networks. They consist of numerous interconnected 
neurons and adjust connection weights through learning 
algorithms to process and analyze data. ANNs have been 
widely applied in various fields, including image recog-
nition, speech recognition, natural language processing, 
financial forecasting, medical diagnosis, and intelligent 
control, providing powerful tools and methods for solv-
ing complex problems [4–7]. Artificial synaptic devices 
have been employed to construct ANNs, extensively study-
ing memristor-based artificial synapses [8–10]. However, 
memristive synaptic devices face high conductance and 
static power consumption, limiting their application in 
neuromorphic computing. Memcapacitors based on the 
capacitance principle have received much attention since 
2009, when researchers suggested that memory storage ele-
ments need not be limited to resistors [11]. On the one hand, 
memcapacitors can store charge and modulate capacitance 
based on voltage. On the other hand, information in these 
devices is transmitted in the form of charge rather than 
current, resulting in lower power consumption and more 
significant application potential. For instance, Bobo Tian 
et al. proposed a ferroelectric polymer-based memcapaci-
tive synaptic model that achieves multivalued capacitance by 
modulating the polarization state of ferroelectric domains, 
thus simulating synaptic weights [12]. Since the discovery 
of ferroelectricity in silicon-doped hafnium oxide ­(HfO2) 
by German scientists in 2011, hafnium-based ferroelectric 
devices have been extensively studied due to their high com-
patibility with CMOS technology, low energy consumption, 
and long-term data retention [13–15]. In recent years, mem-
capacitors based on ­HfO2 ferroelectric thin films have been 
under intensive research and development. Researchers have 
explored the potential of ­HfO2-based ferroelectric capacitors 
to construct artificial synapses by modulating ferroelectric 
polarization, successfully simulating synaptic plasticity 
and performing tasks such as handwritten digit recognition 
[16]. Furthermore, Zuopu Zhou et al. proposed and demon-
strated a crossbar array based on ­HfO2-based ferroelectric 
memcapacitors, showcasing the read and write operations 
of the capacitive array [17]. Meanwhile, flexible electronic 
products are increasingly becoming integral to our daily 
lives. Smart wearable devices, such as electronic skin, are 
under extensive research. Additionally, multifunctional soft 
robots utilized in AI demonstrate highly adaptive interac-
tions with their environment and play significant roles in 
various applications. These advancements depend heavily 
on the development of flexible wearable sensors [18–21]. 
Zhenhai Li et al. investigated artificial synaptic devices 
based on flexible HfAlO ferroelectric tunnel junctions for 
neuromorphic computing, achieving a handwriting recogni-
tion accuracy of 88.8% [22]. Flexible electronics, character-
ized by high flexibility, lightweight, and stretchability, are 
driving innovations in wearable devices, healthcare, and the 
Internet of Things (IoT), making them a key direction for 
the future development of electronic technology [23–25]. 
Based on the future development needs of AI technology, 
integrating additional flexible features into ­HfO2-based fer-
roelectric memcapacitive synaptic devices not only aids in 
constructing low-power neural networks but also facilitates 
the creation of intelligent sensing systems when combined 
with flexible sensing components. Research on multivalued 
storage in ferroelectric memcapacitors primarily focuses 
on modulating the polarization switching of ferroelectric 
domains. Although there is some connection between ferro-
electric polarization and capacitance, it is not a simple direct 
relationship. Thus, there is some bias in using multivalued 
polarization to express capacitance properties.
In this work, we report the fabrication of a flexible mem-
capacitive synaptic device based on Zr-doped ­HfO2 ferro-
electric thin films on mica substrate using low-temperature 
atomic layer deposition (ALD). This device was employed 
for handwritten digit recognition through neural network 
simulation. By comparing the changes in ferroelectric 
remnant polarization (Pr) between flat and bent states, it is 
observed that bending slightly degrades the performance of 
the memcapacitor. Finite element analysis (FEA) simula-
tions of stress variations under different bending radii indi-
cated that a high concentration of oxygen vacancies might be 
the primary cause of performance degradation. Additionally, 
the memcapacitive properties of the device were explored, 
and potentiation and depression of synaptic behaviors were 
successfully demonstrated by simulating synaptic weight 
updates using multivalued capacitance. On these findings, 
a neural network was constructed using memcapacitive 
artificial synapses, and handwritten digit recognition tasks 
were performed using the MNIST dataset provided by the 
National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), with 
a recognition accuracy of 97.63%. These results suggest that 
flexible ­HfO2-based ferroelectric memcapacitive synaptic 
devices contribute to developing high-efficiency neural 
networks and hold significant potential for neuromorphic 
computing applications.
2  Experimental details
First, fluorophlogopite mica was chosen as the flexible 
substrate, and a mica substrate with a thickness of approxi-
mately 30 µm was obtained through mechanical exfoliation.

A 24-nm Pt bottom electrode was deposited on the mica sub-
strate via electron beam evaporation. Low-temperature ALD 
at 100 °C was used to alternately deposit ­HfO2 and ­ZrO2 
layers, forming the Zr-doped ­HfO2 ferroelectric thin film. 
The metal precursors used were TDMAHf and TDMAZr, 
with ­H2O as the oxygen source, and the ­HfO2/ZrO2 cycle 
ratio was 4:3. Subsequently, a 40-nm W top electrode was 
deposited via electron beam evaporation. The top electrode 
pattern, formed using a shadow mask, was circular with a 
diameter of 200 µm. Finally, the sandwich-structured Zr-
doped ­HfO2 ferroelectric capacitor underwent rapid thermal 
annealing at 550 °C for 120 s in an ­N2 environment.
The crystalline structure and elemental composition of 
ferroelectric memcapacitor devices were characterized using 
grazing incidence X-ray diffraction (GIXRD), transmission 
electron microscopy (TEM), and X-ray photoelectron spec-
troscopy (XPS), respectively. The ferroelectric properties 
of the memcapacitors were tested using a ferroelectric ana-
lyzer (TF Analyzer 3000). Additionally, the memcapacitors’ 
leakage current characteristics and memcapacitive properties 
were investigated using a semiconductor analyzer (Keysight 
B1500A). Subsequently, fixed-radius bending molds were 
fabricated via 3D printing for bending tests.

device during compression and tension. Stress concentra-

type (tensile or compressive) does not affect the intensity 
and range of stress distribution after bending. Additionally, 
simulations were conducted to analyze the stress distribu-
tion in the device at bending radii of 10 mm, 12 mm, and 
16 mm. As Figure S3(d)-(f) show, the stress decreases with 
increasing bending radius. GIXRD analysis determined that 
the ­Hf0.56Zr0.44O2 ferroelectric film is polycrystalline, with 
grain boundaries between the grains. Therefore, stress con-
centration induced by bending may generate charged defects, 
such as oxygen vacancies at grain boundaries, causing lat-
tice distortion [30]. Oxygen vacancies are crucial factors 
influencing the polarization state of ferroelectric films. 
High concentrations of oxygen vacancies can pin numer-
ous ferroelectric domains, leading to decreased polarization 
switching speed, reduced ferroelectric polarization intensity, 
and fatigue resistance [31–33]. Figure S2(c) illustrates the 
current leakage density of the device under tensile and flat 
states. The device exhibits higher leakage current under ten-
sile stress, likely due to the increased presence of charged 
defects such as oxygen vacancies in the ­Hf0.56Zr0.44O2 film 
induced during bending. These defects act as shallow traps, 
facilitating more accessible conduction paths and thus 
resulting in elevated leakage current levels [34]. Fig. 2e 
also shows the retention performance for the flat and tensile 
states measured at 4.0 V and 10 kHz, indicating excellent 
retention performance with minimal remnant polarization 
loss after ­104 s. Further analysis using the rational relation 
Pr = P0t−k shows that the 2Pr in the flat and tensile states 
of the devices decayed by 51.8% and 55.7%, respectively, 
after 10 years, where t denotes time since polarization and 
k is a constant linked to the ferroelectric film thickness 
(0.04) [35, 36]. Furthermore, the fatigue characteristics of 
the ­Hf0.56Zr0.44O2 ferroelectric films are depicted in Fig. 2f. 
Applied with ± 4.0 V voltage pulses at 1 MHz, the devices 
demonstrate endurance of at least ­1010 cycles regardless of 
bending, highlighting its potential for flexible ferroelectric 
memory applications.

of the memcapacitor device at 50 kHz under different volt-
ages, where the butterfly curve is observable, indicating 
ferroelectricity. Figure S2(d) and (e) show the capacitance

C-f curves reflect the capacitive response at different fre-
quencies, which is crucial for evaluating its performance in 
high-frequency operations, such as neuromorphic comput-
ing. In this work, we define the memory storage window of 
the memcapacitor as the difference in capacitance (ΔC = 50 
pF) at the same voltage between forward and reverse scans 
in the C-f curve. This definition helps eliminate the influ-
ence of frequency variations on capacitance values. A larger 
storage window indicates that the device can achieve signifi-
cant capacitance changes at different voltages, demonstrat-
ing higher multilevel storage potential, which is suitable for 
synaptic weight update simulations in neuromorphic com-
puting. The inset in Fig. 3b and c indicates that the device 
has a memory storage window of roughly 50 pF and good 
stability. Furthermore, constructing a neuromorphic system 
relies on the simulation and updating of synaptic weights, 
with long-term potentiation (LTP) and long-term depres-
sion (LTD) characteristics being fundamental for simulat-
ing artificial synaptic weights [16, 40]. Fig. 3d demonstrates 
the synaptic plasticity of the ferroelectric memcapacitive 
synapse under pulse amplitude modulation. The inset is a 
schematic diagram of the voltage pulse test, where the pulse 
width is 100 ns, and the pulse interval is 1 µs. The LTP 
process is observed when continuous positive voltages (1 to 
2.5 V, Vread = 0.1 V) are applied to the device. In contrast, 
the LTD process occurs when continuous negative volt-
ages (− 1 to − 2.8 V, Vread = 0.1 V) are used. Additionally, 
the LTP/LTD characteristics of the device under a bending 
radius of 8 mm are also measured, showing similar trends 
to the flat state but with a slight decrease in capacitance 
values. The αp/αd in the flat and tensile states were obtained 
by least squares fitting of the synaptic plasticity curves as 
0.079/0.109 and 0.112/0.044. The central idea when calcu-
lating the asymmetry using the least squares method is to 
quantify the degree of deviation of the actual data from the 
ideal linear relationship by fitting an ideal straight line. The 
specific calculation method is detailed in the Supplementary 
Information. The asymmetry index (AI) of synaptic plastic-
ity is the absolute value of the subtraction of αp from αd. 
The AI = 0.030 at the flat state indicates that the symmetry 
between LTP and LTD is better, which is favorable for the 
linear weight update of the neural network, while the AI 
= 0.068 at the stretched state indicates that the mechanical 
strain leads to an increase in the asymmetry between LTP 
and LTD, which may affect the training efficiency. Multival-
ued capacitance and the successful simulation of LTP/LTD 
characteristics indicate that constructing artificial synapses 
based on ferroelectric capacitance switching is feasible. By 
adjusting the multivalued capacitance changes, synaptic 
weight updates can be simulated, thus enabling recognition 
functions. Additionally, Figure S4(b) illustrates the short-
term plasticity (PPF) of the HZO memcapacitive synaptic 
device. In the experiments, voltage pulses with pulse width 
and pulse interval time of 100 ms were applied to the flex-
ible HZO ferroelectric memcapacitive synaptic device, and 
it was observed that the synaptic response showed a decreas-
ing trend of PPF exponentially with the increase of time, a 
phenomenon that is highly consistent with the short-term 
plasticity behavior in biological synapses, suggesting that 
the devices are able to efficiently mimic the short-term mem-
ory properties of biological synapses. Figure 3e presents 
eight programmable stable capacitance states of memcapaci-
tors, with data sourced from five devices, and each capaci-
tance state is measured five times repeatedly. The modula-
tion pulses for the target capacitance values are consistent 
with the method used in Fig. 3d. We can observe that the 
eight modulated capacitance states, both within individual 
devices through repeated tests and among different devices, 
exhibit excellent consistency. This indicates that the fabri-
cated memcapacitors possess good multi-bit characteristics, 
laying a foundation for their ability to perform non-volatile 
weight storage.

performance advantages of this work [16, 22, 44–46]. The

memcapacitive synaptic devices on flexible substrates. The

4  Conclusion
In this work, Zr-doped ­HfO2 ferroelectric memcapacitive 
synaptic devices were fabricated on a mica substrate. The 
device exhibited a 2Pr of 45.65 µC/cm2 when a 4-V voltage 
was applied in a flat state. The impact of bending on device 
performance was also investigated. Bending resulted in a 
slight decrease in polarization, but the overall effect was 
minimal, with the remnant polarization remaining at a high 
level. FEA indicated that stress concentration caused by 
bending could lead to grain boundary distortion and the gen-
eration of excess oxygen vacancies, resulting in polarization 
reduction. After 10 years, the 2Pr of the devices decayed by 
51.8% and 55.7% in the flat and tensile states, respectively, 
indicating excellent retention characteristics. Addition-
ally, the memcapacitive characteristics of the device were 
studied. The C-V curves at different voltages demonstrated

Abstract: Conventional von Neumann architecture-based computing hardware faces high power consumption challenges and the mis- match between memory and computation performance when handling increasingly large and complex datasets. The rise of artificial neural networks (ANN) has driven the development of bio-inspired memory devices, such as artificial synapses, offering new opportunities to overcome the limitations of the post-Moore era. Ferroelectric memcapacitors, which store data based on capacitive principles, provide advantages such as resistance to read disturbance and low static power consumption compared to memristors, making them highly attractive for ANN applications. In this work, we fabricated Zr-doped ­HfO2 (HZO) ferroelectric memcapacitive synaptic devices on mica substrate featuring a simple metal-ferroelectric-metal struc- ture. We investigated the impact of bending on the ferroelectric performance and, through finite element analysis, found that stress concentration might lead to an increase in grain boundary defects, resulting in excess oxygen vacancies and a slight decrease in ferroelectric polarization. Additionally, we studied the memcapacitive characteristics of the HZO ferroelectric synaptic devices and successfully obtained the potentiation and depression characteristics. The synaptic plasticity curves were also fitted by least squares to obtain asymmetries of 0.030 and 0.068 for the flat and tensile states, respectively. The devices demonstrated remarkable neuromorphic computing capabilities, reaching a digital recognition accuracy as high as 97.63%. Notably, the maximum energy consumption per device was approximately 1.96 nJ in the training process and 4.03 pJ in the inference process. This study provides new directions for further developing flexible hafnium-based ferroelectric materials and devices.
